mcqs.question: A product catalog changes a handful of times per day and a few hours of search staleness is completely acceptable to the business. Which indexing approach fits best?
options: Batch reindexing on a schedule, since the simpler approach is sufficient when staleness is tolerable
Near-real-time indexing via CDC, since freshness should always be maximized
Synchronous dual writes inside every database transaction
No indexing pipeline at all — query the database directly for every search
mcqs.explanation: Batch reindexing is simpler to build and operate, and it's the right choice whenever the product can tolerate the staleness it introduces — building near-real-time infrastructure here would be unnecessary complexity. Direct database queries don't give you the ranking a search engine needs.

mcqs.question: Why is CDC-driven indexing generally more reliable than dual writes for keeping a search index in sync?
options: CDC has zero indexing lag, unlike dual writes
CDC derives updates from the database's own committed change log, so it can't miss a write the way a failed second write can
CDC doesn't require any additional infrastructure to run
Dual writes are always faster, so CDC is only used when speed doesn't matter
mcqs.explanation: Because CDC reads from the database's durable log of committed changes, it structurally can't lose a write the way an application's separate second write can fail independently. CDC does have some lag (not zero) and does require its own infrastructure to run.

mcqs.question: A team changes their search index's tokenizer to better handle a new language. What does this require?
options: Nothing — the new tokenizer applies automatically to already-indexed documents
A full reindex, since existing documents were never processed with the new tokenizer's rules
Only reindexing documents written after the change
mcqs.explanation: Changing the analyzer/tokenizer means every previously indexed document was tokenized under the old rules, so only rebuilding the whole index applies the new rules consistently. A restart or reindexing just new documents leaves old documents indexed inconsistently.

mcqs.question: A team uses dual writes: application code writes to the database, then separately writes to the search index. Months later, some documents are missing from search with no errors ever logged. What's the most likely cause?
options: Some second writes to the index silently failed (crash, timeout, brief outage) with no atomicity between the two writes and no retry
The search index has a hard cap on total document count
The database is corrupting data before it's ever written
Search indexes cannot store more than a few thousand documents reliably
mcqs.explanation: Dual writes aren't atomic — if the second write fails independently of the first, the index silently drifts from the database with nothing forcing a retry, which is exactly the accumulating-gap failure mode described. There's no such document cap or database corruption implied here.
